question: What Should a Proper WordPress Backup Strategy Actually Include?
metaDescription: Both files and database, stored off-server, on a schedule matching content changes — with an actual tested restore, not just backups sitting unused.
shortAnswer: A complete backup needs both the files (themes, plugins, uploads, core) and the database (posts, settings, and for an ecommerce site, orders), stored somewhere other than the same server being backed up, on a schedule that matches how frequently content actually changes. Just as important as taking backups is periodically testing that a restore from them actually works, since an untested backup is only a backup in theory.

image.alt: A complete WordPress backup covering both files and database, stored off-server, with periodic restore testing to confirm it actually works

bodyHtml:
The Two Halves of a Complete Backup

Files and database each hold half the picture — a files-only backup misses every post, page, order, and setting stored in the database, while a database-only backup misses uploaded media, the active theme's customizations, and installed plugins. A genuinely complete backup captures both together, ideally coordinated so they represent the same point in time rather than being backed up on mismatched schedules.

What a Proper Strategy Looks Like

  • Off-server storage is essential — a backup stored on the same server it's protecting doesn't survive a server-level failure, a hosting account issue, or a compromise affecting the whole server, defeating much of the backup's purpose.
  • Backup frequency matching content change frequency — a store taking dozens of orders daily needs much more frequent backups than a mostly-static brochure site updated monthly.
  • Multiple retained backup versions, not just the most recent one, since sometimes a problem (a bad update, a subtle compromise) isn't discovered until after several backups have already been taken, and only an older version predates the issue.
  • Periodic test restores, ideally to a staging environment, confirming the backup actually works and produces a genuinely functional site — this is the step most commonly skipped, and the one that matters most when an actual emergency restore is needed.
  • Database encryption or secure storage, since a backup often contains customer data and needs the same security consideration as the live site itself.

Setting This Up Properly

  1. Choose a backup solution covering both files and database together, storing them off-server.
  2. Set a backup frequency matching the site's actual content/order volume.
  3. Retain multiple historical versions, not just the latest.
  4. Schedule a periodic test restore to confirm the backups genuinely work.
